functions.name: SUM
functions.what: Adds every number in the cells or values you give it. Text and blank cells are skipped.
args: A cell, a range like `B2:B6`, or a number

example.say: B8 adds the maths marks. Change a mark and watch the total update. Then try `=SUM(B2:C6)`.

mistakes: Typing the answer instead of a formula, so it never updates.
Leaving a row out of the range when you add data below it.
Expecting SUM to add text that only looks like a number (it skips it).

functions.name: AVERAGE
functions.what: Adds the numbers and divides by how many numbers there are. Blank cells and text don’t count, so they don’t drag the average down.

example.say: C8 averages science, where Karan is “absent”: the text is skipped, so the average is over four people.

mistakes: Treating a blank as zero: AVERAGE ignores blanks, but a typed 0 counts.
Averaging averages from groups of different sizes.

functions.name: MIN
functions.what: Returns the smallest number in the cells you give it.

example.say: B8 finds the lowest maths mark.

mistakes: MIN of an empty range is 0, not blank.

functions.name: MAX
functions.what: Returns the largest number in the cells you give it.

example.say: B9 shows the spread between the best and worst maths marks.

mistakes: Using MAX on dates gives the latest date, which is often exactly what you want.

functions.name: COUNT
functions.what: Counts the cells that hold numbers (dates count too). Text and blanks are not counted.

example.say: C8 counts science marks: 4, because “absent” is text.

mistakes: Using COUNT to count names: it ignores text. Use COUNTA.

functions.name: COUNTA
functions.what: Counts every cell that isn’t empty: numbers, text, dates, TRUE/FALSE and errors.

example.say: B8 counts the student names.

mistakes: A cell with a space in it looks empty but is counted.

functions.name: COUNTBLANK
functions.what: Counts the empty cells in a range.

example.say: B7 counts students who haven’t paid yet.

mistakes: A formula that returns "" counts as blank.

functions.name: ROUND
functions.what: Rounds a number to the number of decimal places you choose. Formatting only changes how a number looks; ROUND changes the number itself.
args: Decimal places; 0 for whole numbers, -2 for hundreds

example.say: Change B1 and compare B2 and B3.

mistakes: Rounding with the format buttons, then wondering why totals are off by a paisa.

functions.name: ROUNDUP
functions.what: Rounds up to the decimals you choose, for example for packs or boxes needed.

example.say: 53 students at 20 a bus need 3 buses, not 2.65.

mistakes: Using ROUND when you must never fall short.

functions.name: ROUNDDOWN
functions.what: Rounds down to the decimals you choose.

example.say: Only full hours count.

mistakes: ROUNDDOWN(-2.5,0) gives -2: it moves towards zero.

functions.name: INT
functions.what: Rounds a number down to the nearest whole number.

example.say: INT always rounds down, so -7.9 becomes -8.

functions.name: MOD
functions.what: Returns what’s left over after dividing.

example.say: Split students into three groups by roll number.

mistakes: Dividing by 0 gives #DIV/0!.

functions.name: PRODUCT
functions.what: Multiplies all the numbers you give it.

example.say: Same as `=A2*B2`.

mistakes: Blank cells are skipped, not treated as zero.

functions.name: ABS
functions.what: Returns a number without its sign.

example.say: Useful for the size of a gap either way.

functions.name: SQRT
functions.what: Returns the positive square root.
mistakes: A negative number gives #NUM!.

functions.name: POWER
functions.what: Raises a number to a power, same as the ^ operator.

example.say: Compound growth over five years.

functions.name: TODAY
functions.what: Returns today’s date. It updates every time the workbook recalculates.

example.say: Dates are numbers, so you can subtract them.

mistakes: Typing a date with Ctrl+; when you need it fixed, and TODAY() when you need it live, not the other way round.

functions.name: NOW
functions.what: Returns the current date and time.
mistakes: It changes on every recalculation, so don’t use it to stamp when something happened.

functions.name: DATE
functions.what: Makes a real date from a year, month and day.

example.say: Change the month to 13 and see it roll into January 2027.

functions.name: YEAR
functions.what: Returns the year of a date.
mistakes: If the date is really text, YEAR gives #VALUE!.

functions.name: MONTH
functions.what: Returns the month, 1 to 12.

functions.name: DAY
functions.what: Returns the day, 1 to 31.

functions.name: IF
functions.what: Tests a condition and returns one result if it’s TRUE and another if it’s FALSE.
args: Something that is TRUE or FALSE, like `B2>=40`
What to show when it’s true

example.say: Fill D2 down to D6 with the fill handle.

mistakes: Forgetting the quotes around text results.
Testing `B2>50` when 50 should pass.

functions.name: AND
functions.what: Returns TRUE only if every condition is TRUE.

functions.name: OR
functions.what: Returns TRUE if at least one condition is TRUE.

functions.name: NOT
functions.what: Reverses a logical value.

functions.name: IFERROR
functions.what: Returns the formula’s result, or something you choose if it’s an error.
args: What to show instead of an error

example.say: Without IFERROR this would show #DIV/0!.

mistakes: Hiding errors you should be fixing.

functions.name: LEN
functions.what: Returns how many characters are in a text, spaces included.

example.say: Extra spaces count, which is how LEN finds them.

functions.name: LEFT
functions.what: Returns the first characters of a text.

example.say: The state code from a vehicle number.

functions.name: RIGHT
functions.what: Returns the last characters of a text.

functions.name: MID
functions.what: Returns characters starting at a position.

functions.name: UPPER
functions.what: Changes text to capitals.

functions.name: LOWER
functions.what: Changes text to lower case.

functions.name: PROPER
functions.what: Capitalises the first letter of each word.
mistakes: Names like McDonald or MBA come out as Mcdonald and Mba.

functions.name: TRIM
functions.what: Removes spaces from the start and end, and turns double spaces into single ones.

functions.name: CONCAT
functions.what: Joins text from cells or ranges.

example.say: Same as `=A1&" "&B1`.

functions.name: TEXT
functions.what: Turns a number into text in a format you choose.
args: A format code in quotes, like "dd-mmm-yyyy"
mistakes: The result is text, so you can’t do maths with it.

functions.name: VALUE
functions.what: Turns text that looks like a number into a real number.

functions.name: SUMIF
functions.what: Adds the numbers that meet one condition.

functions.name: COUNTIF
functions.what: Counts the cells that meet one condition.

functions.name: AVERAGEIF
functions.what: Averages the cells that meet one condition.

functions.name: IFS
functions.what: Checks tests in order and returns the answer paired with the first one that is TRUE. End with TRUE as a catch-all.
args: What to show if test1 is TRUE
More pairs; TRUE as the last test catches everything else

example.say: Change A2 to 95 or 40 and watch the grade change.

mistakes: Putting the lowest band first: everyone stops at it.
No catch-all: unmatched values show #N/A.

functions.name: SWITCH
functions.what: Compares one value with a list of exact matches and returns the matching result, or a default.
args: A value to match and what to show

example.say: Try C, K or X in A2.

mistakes: Using it for ranges like 75 and above: SWITCH only matches exact values.

functions.name: IFNA
functions.what: Returns the value, or your fallback if it is #N/A. Other errors still show.

example.say: P09 isn’t in the list. Change it to P01.

mistakes: Using IFERROR around lookups hides real mistakes like #REF!.

functions.name: XOR
functions.what: Returns TRUE when an odd number of its tests are TRUE: for two tests, exactly one.

example.say: TRUE when someone works one shift but not both.

functions.name: FIND
functions.what: Returns where one piece of text first appears inside another. Capitals matter.
args: What to look for, in quotes

example.say: Use the position with LEFT or MID to cut the text.

mistakes: Not found gives #VALUE!.

functions.name: SEARCH
functions.what: Like FIND, but ignores capitals and allows wildcards: ? for one character, * for any run.

example.say: ISNUMBER(SEARCH(…)) is a handy “contains” test.

mistakes: Not found gives #VALUE!.

functions.name: SUBSTITUTE
functions.what: Replaces every copy of some text with other text; "" deletes it.

example.say: Nested: spaces first, then dashes.

mistakes: It’s case-sensitive.

functions.name: REPLACE
functions.what: Replaces a number of characters starting at a position.

example.say: Show only the last four digits.

functions.name: CLEAN
functions.what: Removes line breaks and other non-printing characters, often pasted from other systems.

example.say: Combine with TRIM: =TRIM(CLEAN(A2)).

functions.name: TEXTJOIN
functions.short: Join a range with a separator
functions.what: Joins text from cells or ranges, putting a separator between them, and can skip empty cells.

example.say: The empty landmark is skipped.

mistakes: FALSE keeps blanks and leaves “, ,” gaps.

functions.name: TEXTSPLIT
functions.what: Splits text at a separator; the pieces spill into the cells beside it (or below, with a row separator).

example.say: The three pieces spill into B4:D4.

mistakes: Something in the way of the pieces gives #SPILL!.

functions.name: TEXTBEFORE
functions.what: Returns the text before a delimiter; a negative instance counts from the end.

example.say: Simpler than LEFT with FIND.

mistakes: Not found gives #N/A unless you set if_not_found.

functions.name: TEXTAFTER
functions.what: Returns the text after a delimiter; -1 means after the last one.

example.say: −1 takes what follows the last comma.

functions.name: REPT
functions.what: Repeats text a number of times; handy for quick in-cell bars.

example.say: A tiny bar chart in a cell.

functions.name: EXACT
functions.what: Returns TRUE only if two texts match exactly, capitals included.

example.say: = ignores capitals; EXACT doesn’t.

functions.name: NUMBERVALUE
functions.what: Converts number-looking text to a number, with the decimal and group separators you name.

example.say: European style becomes 1234.5.

functions.name: LARGE
functions.what: Returns the 1st, 2nd, 3rd… largest number.

functions.name: SMALL
functions.what: Returns the 1st, 2nd, 3rd… smallest number.

functions.name: MEDIAN
functions.what: Returns the middle number: half are above, half below. Less pulled by extremes than AVERAGE.

example.say: One huge salary pulls the average up; the median barely moves.

functions.name: RANK.EQ
functions.what: Returns a number’s rank in a list (1 = largest by default).

example.say: Lock the list with $ before filling down.

mistakes: Forgetting $ on the list, so it slides as you fill down.

shortcuts.what: Jump to the edge of the data (down)
Jump to the edge of the data (right)
Go to the last used cell
Go To a cell or name
Select to the end of the data
Extend the selection by one cell
Start a new line inside a cell

glossary: A value you give a function inside its brackets, like the range in =SUM(B2:B9).
A function used as an argument of another; Excel works it out first.
When one formula’s answer fills several cells below or beside it, with a dashed blue border.
Formulas › Evaluate Formula: steps through a formula one part at a time.
Automatic recalculates on every change; Manual waits for F9.
A TRUE or FALSE value. In maths, TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0.
The character that separates pieces of text, like the comma in a list.
Looks like a number but is text: it sits on the left and SUM ignores it.
An Excel file. It holds one or more worksheets.
One grid of cells, shown as a tab at the bottom.
One box in the grid, named by its column and row, like **B4**.
A block of cells, written first:last, like **B2:D10**.
A calculation that starts with **=**, like `=B2*C2`.
A named calculation Excel already knows, like SUM or AVERAGE.
A value a function needs, inside its brackets.
The address of a cell or range used in a formula.
A reference like `B2` that moves when you copy the formula.
A reference like `$B$2` that stays fixed when you copy.
Only the row or only the column is fixed, like `B$2` or `$B2`.
A name like **TaxRate** that stands for a cell or range.
The small square at the bottom-right of a selection; drag it to copy or continue a series.
Continuing a pattern (numbers, dates, months) by dragging the fill handle.
Excel fills a column by copying a pattern you type once (Ctrl+E).
The band of tabs and buttons at the top of the window.
The box left of the formula bar; it shows the active cell and lets you jump to any cell.
Shows the real contents of the active cell, including formulas.
The bar at the bottom; it shows Sum, Average and Count of the selection.
The File menu: save, open, print, share and export.
A range turned into a Table (Ctrl+T): it has a name, filter buttons and grows by itself.
Rules that control what can be typed in a cell, such as a drop-down list.
How a number is shown (₹, %, dates) without changing its value.
Keeps rows or columns visible while you scroll.
A formula result that fills several cells (dynamic arrays).
